---
title: "Bonus: exploring the whole corpus without downloading it"
format: html
---

*Optional, not part of the class exercise.*

In section 9 of the lab you thought about asking a question of Climate Policy Radar's **whole**
corpus: every national climate law and policy and every UNFCCC submission in its database. This
notebook goes back to the cloud-native workflow from Module 1 (the GBIF notebook) and applies it to
that corpus: describing it, slicing it, drawing a fair sample of passages the experts never
labelled, and (optionally) running the lab's model on them.

## Why not just download it?

The full-text dataset is 48 Parquet files, about 3.6 GB compressed, with tens of millions of rows
(one per text block: a paragraph, heading or table cell as laid out in the original document).
You could download it, but:

- It's slow, and it fills your disk. Uncompressed in memory it would be several times larger, more
  than most laptops have
- Most questions don't need most of it. "How many documents per country?" needs two small columns,
  not the full text of every page
- Every copy is a snapshot that goes out of date, and someone has to store it

Module 1 queried GBIF (about 500 GB) in minutes by never downloading it. The same tricks apply here:

| Technique | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Columnar storage (Parquet)** | Each column is stored separately, so a query reads only the columns it uses |
| **HTTP range requests** | DuckDB asks the server for specific byte ranges of a file, not the whole file |
| **File metadata** | Every Parquet file ends with a small footer listing its columns, row counts and sizes |
| **Filtering early** | Rows that don't match a filter are dropped as the data streams in |

## Setup

The dataset is free but gated:

1. Make a free account at <https://huggingface.co>
2. Accept the terms at <https://huggingface.co/datasets/ClimatePolicyRadar/all-document-text-data>
3. Check the dataset page now says you have access (not a form, and not "pending")
4. Create a token of type **Read** (profile picture > Settings > Access Tokens). A "fine-grained"
   token only works if you tick "Read access to contents of all public gated repos you can access"
5. Add `HF_TOKEN=hf_...` to your `.Renviron` file (`usethis::edit_r_environ()`), then restart R.
   You might need to install the `usethis` package (`install.packages("usethis")`)

::: {.callout-warning}
## The most common problem: the wrong kind of token

If you see an error like `HTTP GET error ... (HTTP 0 Internal Server Error)`, your token is almost
certainly being refused. Hugging Face's default token type is **fine-grained**, and a fine-grained
token can't read gated datasets unless you tick **"Read access to contents of all public gated
repos you can access"** when you create it. The easy fix is to create a new token and choose the
**Read** tab instead. Then update `HF_TOKEN` in `.Renviron` and restart R.
:::

```{r setup}
# install.packages(c("duckdb", "DBI", "dplyr", "dbplyr", "ggplot2", "jsonlite", "curl"))
install.packages("duckdb")   # then restart R
packageVersion("duckdb")     # should be 1.3 or later
library(DBI)
library(duckdb)
library(dplyr)     # the same verbs you use on data frames: filter, group_by, summarise, ...
library(dbplyr)    # lets those verbs run inside DuckDB instead of in R
library(ggplot2)


# An in-memory DuckDB database. Nothing is stored on disk.
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())

# Reading files from Hugging Face needs a recent DuckDB (1.3 or later). If this stops you,
# run install.packages("duckdb") and restart R.
if (packageVersion("duckdb") < "1.3.0") {
  stop("Your duckdb package is version ", packageVersion("duckdb"),
       ". Please update it: install.packages(\"duckdb\"), then restart R.", call. = FALSE)
}

# httpfs lets DuckDB read files over the internet (as in Module 1). It is downloaded once,
# the first time you run this.
invisible(dbExecute(con, "INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;"))

# Use DuckDB's curl-based downloader, which copes better with how Hugging Face serves files
# (it redirects to a separate storage server) and with certificates on some laptops.
invisible(try(dbExecute(con, "SET httpfs_client_implementation = 'curl'"), silent = TRUE))

# Give DuckDB your Hugging Face token so it can read the gated files. The token is read from your
# environment and never printed.
token <- Sys.getenv("HF_TOKEN")
if (token == "") stop("No HF_TOKEN found. See the setup steps above.", call. = FALSE)
invisible(dbExecute(con, paste0("CREATE SECRET hf (TYPE HUGGINGFACE, TOKEN '", token, "')")))

# All 48 files, addressed with a wildcard. hf:// is DuckDB's shortcut for Hugging Face datasets.
FILES <- "hf://datasets/ClimatePolicyRadar/all-document-text-data/*.parquet"

# Quick check that we can reach one file before doing anything bigger.
check <- try(dbGetQuery(con, paste0(
  "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM parquet_file_metadata('",
  sub("*.parquet", "train_0.parquet", FILES, fixed = TRUE), "')")), silent = TRUE)
if (inherits(check, "try-error")) {
  # DuckDB reports a refused token as "HTTP 0", so ask Hugging Face directly what's wrong.
  h <- curl::new_handle(nobody = TRUE)
  curl::handle_setheaders(h, Authorization = paste("Bearer", token))
  status <- curl::curl_fetch_memory(
    "https://huggingface.co/datasets/ClimatePolicyRadar/all-document-text-data/resolve/main/train_0.parquet",
    handle = h)$status_code
  if (status %in% c(401, 403)) {
    stop("Hugging Face refused your token (HTTP ", status, "). Check that the dataset page says you ",
         "have access, and that HF_TOKEN is a 'Read' token (or a fine-grained token with access to ",
         "public gated repos). Restart R after changing .Renviron.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  stop("Couldn't read the corpus from Hugging Face (your token looks fine, HTTP ", status, "). ",
       "The original error was:\n", check, call. = FALSE)
}

# The expert-labelled passages we used in the lab (small and public), so we can leave them out later.
LABELLED <- paste0("https://huggingface.co/datasets/ClimatePolicyRadar/national-climate-targets/",
                   "resolve/refs%2Fconvert%2Fparquet/default/train/0000.parquet")
```

### How dplyr works on remote data

`tbl()` gives you something that looks like a data frame but is really a pointer to the files.
dplyr verbs on it don't run in R: dbplyr translates them into a database query, and DuckDB runs
that query against the files, fetching only what it needs. **Nothing is downloaded until you call
`collect()`**, which brings the (small) result into R as an ordinary data frame.

```{r tables}
# The corpus itself: one row per text block, across all 48 files. Nothing is read yet.
corpus_raw <- tbl(con, sql(paste0("SELECT * FROM read_parquet('", FILES, "')")))

# The files' metadata footers: one row per column per chunk of each file.
footers <- tbl(con, sql(paste0("SELECT * FROM parquet_metadata('", FILES, "')")))

# The expert-labelled passages from the lab.
labelled <- tbl(con, sql(paste0("SELECT text FROM read_parquet('", LABELLED, "')")))
```

## 1. How big is it? Read only the footers

Each Parquet file's footer says how many rows it has and how many bytes each column takes up.
DuckDB can read just the footers: a few kilobytes per file, not 3.6 GB.

```{r footers}
t <- system.time(
  meta <- footers |>
    group_by(column_name = path_in_schema) |>
    summarise(bytes = sum(total_compressed_size, na.rm = TRUE),
              rows = sum(row_group_num_rows, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    arrange(desc(bytes)) |>
    collect()                     # run the query and bring the result into R
)
cat("Rows:", format(max(meta$rows), big.mark = ","), "\n")
cat("Total size:", round(sum(meta$bytes) / 1e9, 2), "GB compressed\n")
cat("Time to find out:", round(t[["elapsed"]], 1), "seconds\n")
```

Which columns take up the space? (`meta` is now an ordinary data frame in R.)

```{r column-sizes}
#| fig-height: 5
meta |>
  mutate(share = bytes / sum(bytes)) |>
  slice_max(bytes, n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = reorder(column_name, share))) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Share of the dataset's bytes", y = NULL,
       title = "The 15 largest columns") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

**Think:** if your question only needs the country and document type columns, roughly what share
of the dataset does DuckDB actually have to fetch?

## 2. Look at the columns and tidy them

Listing the columns also reads only the footers.

```{r schema}
colnames(corpus_raw)
```

Column names look like `document_metadata.geographies`. Depending on how the files were written,
that's either one column with a dot in its name or a field inside a `document_metadata` column.
Either way they're awkward to type, so we rename them once. This is the one place we need a
little SQL: `col()` writes the right reference for either case, and `sql()` hands it to DuckDB.

```{r tidy}
col <- function(name) {
  if (name %in% colnames(corpus_raw)) return(paste0('"', name, '"'))     # one column, dot in its name
  parts <- strsplit(name, ".", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  if (parts[1] %in% colnames(corpus_raw)) return(paste(parts, collapse = "."))  # field inside a column
  stop("Column not found: ", name)
}

# Countries should be stored as a list (a document can belong to several). If they turn out to be
# stored as text instead, split them on commas so the code below still works.
geo_type <- corpus_raw |>
  transmute(t = sql(paste0("typeof(", col("document_metadata.geographies"), ")"))) |>
  head(1) |>
  collect()
geo_sql <- if (grepl("\\[\\]", geo_type$t)) col("document_metadata.geographies") else
  paste0("string_split(", col("document_metadata.geographies"), ", ',')")

# A tidy version of the corpus with short column names. Still nothing is read: DuckDB only
# fetches the columns that a later query actually uses.
corpus <- corpus_raw |>
  transmute(
    document_id = sql(col("document_id")),
    title       = sql(col("document_metadata.document_title")),
    corpus_type = sql(col("document_metadata.corpus_type_name")),
    category    = sql(col("document_metadata.category")),
    geographies = sql(geo_sql),
    year        = sql(paste0("year(TRY_CAST(", col("document_metadata.publication_ts"), " AS TIMESTAMP))")),
    translated  = sql(paste0("TRY_CAST(", col("document_metadata.translated"), " AS BOOLEAN)")),
    block_type  = sql(col("text_block.type")),
    language    = sql(col("text_block.language")),
    text        = sql(col("text_block.text"))
  )
```

## 3. Describe the whole corpus from a few small columns

How many documents are there of each type? This reads only three small columns, across all 48
files. Watch the time.

```{r doc-types}
t <- system.time(
  doc_types <- corpus |>
    group_by(corpus_type, category) |>
    summarise(documents = n_distinct(document_id), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(documents)) |>
    collect()
)
doc_types
cat("Seconds:", round(t[["elapsed"]], 1), "\n")
```

Curious what dbplyr sent to DuckDB? `show_query()` prints the translation instead of running it.

```{r show-query}
corpus |>
  group_by(corpus_type, category) |>
  summarise(documents = n_distinct(document_id), .groups = "drop") |>
  show_query()
```

Which countries have the most documents? A document can list several countries, so we `unnest()`
the list first, giving one row per document and country. (`unnest()` isn't an R function here:
dbplyr passes it straight to DuckDB.)

```{r countries}
countries <- corpus |>
  transmute(document_id, geography = unnest(geographies)) |>
  group_by(geography) |>
  summarise(documents = n_distinct(document_id)) |>
  arrange(desc(documents)) |>
  collect()

cat(nrow(countries), "countries or groupings\n")
head(countries, 20)
```

**Think:** compare the most and least represented countries. If you trained or validated a model
on this corpus, whose policies would it learn most from?

When were the documents published, and how much was machine-translated?

```{r years}
#| fig-height: 3.5
by_year <- corpus |>
  distinct(document_id, year) |>
  count(year) |>
  collect()

ggplot(filter(by_year, !is.na(year)), aes(x = year, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Publication year", y = "Documents") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

corpus |>
  distinct(document_id, translated) |>
  summarise(share_translated = mean(as.numeric(translated), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  collect()
```

What kinds of text blocks are there? Only some are running text; the rest are headings, table
cells and so on.

```{r block-types}
corpus |> count(block_type, sort = TRUE) |> collect()
```

## 4. Slice: fetch the text for just what you need

Now a slice with text in it: every text block from one country's documents. DuckDB still reads
the small country column everywhere, but only fetches text where it needs to.

```{r slice}
# ✏️ Pick a country (three-letter ISO code) and a start year
MY_COUNTRY <- "CHE"
FROM_YEAR  <- 2015

t <- system.time(
  slice <- corpus |>
    filter(list_contains(geographies, MY_COUNTRY),   # list_contains() is also a DuckDB function
           year >= FROM_YEAR) |>
    select(document_id, title, category, year, block_type, text) |>
    collect()
)
cat(nrow(slice), "text blocks from", n_distinct(slice$document_id), "documents in",
    round(t[["elapsed"]], 1), "seconds\n")
slice |> count(title, year, sort = TRUE) |> head(10)
```

A slice this size is easy to save and work with locally, for example to hand-code a sample:

```{r save-slice}
readr::write_csv(slice, paste0("data/slice_", MY_COUNTRY, ".csv"))
```

**Think:** was this slice faster or slower than section 3? Some datasets are stored in folders by
country or year, so a query can skip whole folders it doesn't need. This corpus isn't organised by
country, so DuckDB has to check the country column in every file. How data is laid out decides
which questions are cheap to ask.
